text: Concept Bottleneck Models.

From black-box predictions to
interpretable, editable concepts.
A neural network makes a prediction.

How can a person inspect, and correct,
the intermediate evidence it used?

Here is a photograph of a
gull, and a real model, CLIP.

It is asked to choose
among six gull species,

by comparing the image with
a short description of each.

Image in, an encoder, and
a score for every species.

It prefers American herring gull,
with a softmax share of 0.54.

Glaucous-winged gull
comes second, at 0.21.
The answer happens to be right.
But what made the model prefer it?
A common response is a heatmap.

This one is computed: we grey out one
patch of the photograph at a time,

and measure how much the
herring gull score drops.

The largest drops sit on
the bill and the head.
So what did the model recognise there?
The yellow bill?
The red spot near its tip?
The shape of the head?
Or the blue water just behind it?

The map marks where
the score is sensitive.

It does not say which
property the model detected,

and it gives a person
nothing specific to correct.

Suppose instead the model had to state
its evidence as named properties:
wingtip colour, bill shape, head colour.
Each claim could then be checked.

There are two ways to get an
explanation from a model.

You can train a black box and explain it
afterwards, which is called post-hoc.

Or you can build the model so that its
reasoning can be read from the start,

which is called ante-hoc,
or interpretable by design.
Start with post-hoc.
The model f is already trained.

An explanation method takes
the model and one input,

and returns some evidence
about the prediction.
One family asks which pixels mattered.

A saliency map takes the gradient of the
class score with respect to each pixel:

how much the score would
change if that pixel changed.
A second family changes the input.

Grey out one patch, run the model again,
and measure how much the score drops.

That is the occlusion map we
computed for the gull in Part 1.

A third family asks
about concepts directly.

Testing with concept activation vectors,
or TCAV, asks a question like this one:

does the model use grey wings
when it says herring gull?

Here the model is CLIP,
the black box from Part 1.

The first step is to collect example
photos: some birds with grey wings,

and some without, here from
a labelled bird dataset.
None of them is a herring gull.

Pass every photo through the model
and look at its internal activations.
Fit a line that separates the two groups.

The direction across that line is
the concept activation vector:
moving along it means more grey wing.
Now take a herring gull photo and ask:

if its activation moved a little
in the grey wing direction,
would the herring gull score go up?

The gradient of the score, times the
direction, gives the answer as a sign.

The TCAV score is the share of herring
gull photos where the score goes up.

For grey wings, it went up
for almost all 60 photos,

in each of 10 repeats with
different example photos.

A direction that separates two random sets
of photos gives scores that jump between
zero and one.

So a concept counts only when its score
is steady and different from random ones.

And even then, TCAV says
what the model responds to.
It gives no way to correct it.

These methods are useful,
and they have limits.
The first is a sanity check.

If an explanation really
describes the model,
it should change when the model changes.

Adebayo and colleagues tested this by
randomising a trained network's weights,

layer by layer, until
it had learned nothing.

Some saliency methods, such
as guided backpropagation,

still produced almost the same
maps for the randomised network.

Those maps mostly trace the edges in
the image, like an edge detector.

So a convincing map is not, on
its own, evidence about the model.

Plain gradients and Grad-CAM
did pass this test.
The second limit is about shortcuts.

Zech and colleagues trained a pneumonia
detector on chest X-rays from two hospital
systems.

At one hospital about a third
of the patients had pneumonia,
and at the other about one in a hundred.

A network could tell which hospital
an X-ray came from almost perfectly,

from markers and scanner details
rather than from the lungs.
Since the hospital predicts pneumonia,

the detector could use the
hospital as a shortcut.

A heatmap might light up the hospital marker
in the corner, and expose the shortcut.
But it cannot remove it.

On X-rays from a third hospital,
the detector did worse.
The only fix was new data and retraining.
The third limit is vocabulary.

A heatmap says where
the score was sensitive.
It does not say what the model saw there.

On the gull: the yellow bill, the
red spot, or the shape of the head?

Experts reason in named findings: a
narrowed joint space, a bone spur,
black wingtips.

Even when an expert spots the mistake,
the model has no named part to correct.

There is no setting for wingtip colour
that a person could switch from grey to
black.
Ante-hoc models take the other route.

The prediction is computed from
quantities a person can read.

A sparse linear model on
named features is one example.
A short decision tree is another.

Prototype networks compare parts of
an image with stored example parts.

Rudin argued that for high-stakes decisions
we should prefer models like these over
black boxes explained afterwards.

A concept bottleneck model is an
ante-hoc model for deep networks.

First, predict named properties
of the photo, its concepts.

Then predict the answer
from those concepts alone.

In symbols: x is the input, c hat is
the vector of predicted concepts,
and y hat is the prediction.
A concept predictor, g, maps x to c hat.
A task head, f, maps c hat to y hat.

Here is that idea on a real photograph,
with numbers small enough to follow.

Between the image and the answer, we
insert a layer of named variables.

A concept predictor, g theta, maps the
image to a vector of concept values, c hat.

A task head, f phi, maps those
values to the prediction, y hat.

Here the concepts are wingtip grey,
wingtip black, bill pointed, head white,
and tail rounded.
Each receives a value between 0 and 1.

The essential rule: the task head
receives only these five numbers.
No other path from the image reaches it.
That narrow interface is the bottleneck.

A black box maps the image
straight to an answer.

A strict concept bottleneck model,
or CBM, first predicts the concepts,

then predicts the task
from the concepts alone.

These concept values and this head
are written by hand, for teaching.

This model believes the wingtips are
grey, at 0.8, and black, at only 0.2.

So it ranks glaucous-winged
gull first, 0.71 against 0.29.

Look at the photograph:
the wingtips are black.

An observer corrects the
wing colour concepts.
Grey becomes 0, and black becomes 1.
The task head is unchanged.

It simply recomputes, and American
herring gull now receives 0.91.

A person edited an intermediate
belief, and the prediction followed.

Compare multi-task learning, where a
concept head sits beside the class head.

Editing that concept output changes nothing,
because the class head never reads it.

In a concept bottleneck, the concepts
lie on the path to the prediction.
The gull is not a random choice.

The standard benchmark for concept
bottlenecks is a bird dataset:
Caltech-UCSD Birds, or CUB.
It has 11,788 photographs of 200 species.
Eight of the species are gulls.

People annotated every photograph with
312 yes-or-no attributes, in 28 groups:

bill shape, wing colour, wing
pattern, eye colour, and so on.

Each attribute is a question
with a yes or no answer.
Does this bird have a hooked bill?
Is its wing grey?
Yes is a one, and no is a zero.

Annotators also recorded how sure they
were: definitely, probably, guessing,
or not visible.
About one label in ten is not visible.
Labels on single photos are noisy,

so Koh and colleagues took a
majority vote within each species.

After the vote, every photo of a
herring gull has the same labels.

They then kept the 112 attributes that
are present in at least ten species.

One training record is a photograph,
112 zeros and ones, and a species.

In symbols, the concept labels c form a
vector with 112 entries, each zero or one,
and the label y is one of 200 species.

The model predicts c hat, a value
between zero and one for each concept.
Let us slow down.
What exactly is a concept?

It is more than a neuron
with a name attached:

it is a promise that a person
can check the claim in the input.
Three things must be in place.

The first is meaning: a definition
that a domain expert can apply.

For example, grey wingtip: the tips of
the folded flight feathers are grey,
not black.

The second is grounding: where
in the input is the evidence?
For wingtip colour, it is this region.

The estimate should depend on these
feathers, and not on the water or the rock.

The third is representation: how
the concept becomes a number.

The simplest is binary:
c j is zero or one.

A soft concept passes a logit,
z, through the sigmoid,
giving a value between zero and one.
A logit of 1.4 gives 0.80.

A soft score of 0.8 is not
automatically a calibrated probability.

Whether eighty percent of such cases really
have grey wingtips has to be checked on
data.
Some concepts are categorical.
Wing colour takes one value from a list,

so its scores form a softmax over
the options, and they sum to one.

Others are continuous, such as bill length
in millimetres, predicted by regression.

Richer models give each
concept a vector, an embedding,
or a whole probability distribution.
We will meet these in Part 10.
And sometimes the evidence is missing.

In CUB, a wingtip hidden behind
a rock is labelled not visible.

Unknown is not the same as absent, and the
representation should be able to say so.

So a concept can be stored in six ways:
binary, soft, categorical, continuous,
a vector or distribution, and unknown.
The same pattern applies across sensors.

In a sleep EEG recording, a concept
might be: sleep spindle present.

A spindle is a brief burst of brain
waves, about 11 to 16 cycles per second,

lasting roughly half a
second to two seconds.

Sleep scorers treat spindles
as a sign of stage two sleep.

In a customer message, a concept
might be: duplicate charge reported,

meaning the customer says one
purchase was billed twice.

Each is a named claim about the
input that a specialist could check.
How do concept values become an answer?

In the simplest case, the task head is
arithmetic small enough to do by hand.
Three classes: zebra, horse, and giraffe.

Three concepts: stripes,
horse-like shape, and long neck.

Given this low-contrast photograph, the
concept predictor reports stripes 0.1,
horse-like shape 0.9, and long neck 0.1.

Stacked in a column, they form
the concept vector, c hat.

The task head is a weight matrix,
W, with one row per class.

The zebra row holds 3 for stripes, 1 for
horse-like shape, and 0 for long neck.

With all three rows: stripes count toward
zebra, a long neck toward giraffe,
and horse-like shape mostly toward horse.

To score zebra, multiply each weight
by its concept value, and add.
Zebra scores 1.2.
Horse: −0.1, plus 1.8, −0.1, giving 1.6.

Giraffe: −0.1, plus 0,
plus 0.3, giving 0.2.
These are the class scores, or logits.

The largest score is 1.6,
so the model says horse.

A softmax turns the scores into shares
that sum to one: horse gets about 0.52.

Now an observer looks at
the image and sees stripes.

They change one coordinate:
stripes, from 0.1 to 1.
Recompute with the same matrix.

Zebra: 3, plus 0.9, plus
0, which gives 3.9.
Horse: −1, plus 1.8, −0.1, giving 0.7.

Giraffe: −1, plus 0,
plus 0.3, giving −0.7.

After the softmax, zebra leads,
with a share of about 0.95.

The image did not change,
and neither did the matrix.

Each concept value scales
its own column of W.

Only stripes moved, by 0.9, so the scores
moved by 0.9 times the stripes column:

plus 2.7 for zebra, and
−0.9 for the other two.

So a person corrected one of the model's
beliefs, and nothing had to be retrained.
So far the concept values were given.
Where do they come from?

The concept predictor learns
them from labelled examples.

Each training example carries three
things: an input x i, concept labels c i,
and a task label y i.

For a herring gull in CUB: the photo,
zeros and ones, and the species.

The concept loss, L c, compares the
predicted concepts with the labels:

typically a binary cross-entropy
for each concept, averaged.

One term: grey wing has label 1;
suppose the predictor says 0.8.
The term is −log 0.8, about 0.22.
Closer to 1 costs less.

The task loss, L y, is typically
a cross-entropy over the classes:

minus the log of the share
given to the correct class.

A weighted sum combines the two; lambda
c and lambda y set how much each counts.

In the original paper, Koh and
colleagues compared three ways to train.

Independent: fit the predictor
to the concept labels,

and separately fit the
head on the true concepts.

At test time, though, the head
receives predicted concepts.
Sequential: fit the predictor, freeze it,

then fit the head on the
concepts it predicts.

The head learns from the
predictor's actual mistakes.

Joint: train the whole system
at once, with both losses.
In joint training,

the task loss sends its gradient back
through the head and the concept values into

the predictor, which is then
shaped by what helps the task.
That can improve task accuracy.
It can also hurt concept fidelity,

if a concept score drifts toward
whatever helps the classifier.
That has to be measured.

The experiment we will meet
later used joint training,

with the concept loss weighted
2 and the task loss weighted 1.
Part 5 described three training schemes.

Does the choice matter
on real photographs?
We ran a small version on CUB.

Each photo goes through a frozen CLIP
image encoder, giving 512 features.

A linear concept predictor
maps them to 112 concepts,

and a linear task head
maps those to 200 species.
For our gull photo,

the predictor is sure the throat
is white and the wings are grey.

The head spreads its probability
over several gull species.

Joint training is the most accurate, close
to a standard model with no bottleneck.

Sequential falls in between, and
independent training is the least accurate.
Now intervene.

Pick a few attribute groups, replace their
predicted values with the true values,
and let the same head recompute.
The independent model improves fastest.

Its head was trained on true
concepts, so it trusts corrected ones.
The joint model improves least.

Its head learned to read fine
detail in the soft scores,

beyond what the concepts mean, so
a corrected value helps it less.
We will meet this again as leakage.

Koh and colleagues report the same
pattern with fully trained networks.

Concepts are useful because
a person can check them.

When the model gets one wrong, someone
who can see the mistake can correct it,
with no retraining.
An intervention has four steps.
The model predicts concept values.
A person checks one and corrects it.
The fixed task head recomputes.
A new prediction comes out.
Back to the gull.

Wing colour is a categorical concept, so
the observer corrects the group together:
grey to 0, black to 1.

Changing only one of them could leave an
impossible state, with both colours on,
or neither.

The head's score for American
herring gull moves from 0.29 to 0.91.
The same mechanism works on a signal.
Here is a schematic EEG trace,

drawn for teaching rather
than recorded from a patient.

Near the middle is a short burst at about
13 hertz, the shape of a sleep spindle.

The concept predictor gives
spindle present only 0.12.

K-complex present gets 0.8,
and slow-wave dominance 0.15.

With these values, an illustrative
stage head favours other stage, at 0.62,
over an N2 candidate, at 0.38.

A sleep expert inspects the trace
and marks the spindle as present.
0.12 becomes 1.
Same head, new input.
The N2 candidate rises to 0.86.

This demonstrates the mechanism,
not a clinical result.

Real sleep staging applies scoring
rules to thirty-second epochs,
and this head was written by hand.
So far, every correction has helped.
Does a correct edit always help?
Here is a case where it does not.

A support message reads: The app
works, but I was charged twice.
Please refund the extra payment.
It belongs in the billing queue.

The concept predictor rates duplicate charge
at only 0.2, and refund requested at 1.
The task head computes a billing score.

It starts at 1.2, takes away 2
for each unit of duplicate charge,

and adds 0.6 for each
unit of refund requested.

In symbols, the score s is 1.2,
−2 times duplicate charge,
plus 0.6 times refund requested.

A sigmoid turns that score
into the billing share.

Before any edit, the score is 1.2,
−0.4, plus 0.6, which gives 1.4.

Billing receives 0.80, so the
message is already routed correctly.

A reviewer reads the message and
correctly sets duplicate charge to 1.

Now the score is 1.2, −2,
plus 0.6, which gives −0.2.

Billing falls to 0.45, and the
message goes to general support.
The edit was correct.

The fault lies downstream: this head learned
a negative weight for duplicate charge,
the wrong sign for billing.

Correcting a concept does not
repair an incorrect decision rule.

An intervention is only as good
as the head that receives it,

so its effect has to be
measured rather than assumed.

This head was built faulty on purpose,
to show that the failure can happen.
It says nothing about how often it does.

A second limit sits in
the vocabulary itself:

the bottleneck passes on
only what we chose to name.

Take two objects, a blue
circle and a blue square.
They belong to different classes.

Suppose the concept vocabulary has
only two entries: colour and size.
Both objects are blue.
Both are small.

So both map to exactly
the same concept vector.

c of x 1 equals c of x 2,
and yet y 1 differs from y 2.
Watch what reaches the task head.
Shape was present in the image.
At the bottleneck, it disappears.

Any task head that reads only this vector
must give both objects the same output.
No head, linear or a large neural network,

can recover a distinction
that never reached it.

On these two examples, the best
possible accuracy is fifty percent.
The ideal property is called sufficiency.

Once the concepts are known, the input
says nothing more about the label.

In symbols: Y is
independent of X, given C.

Here it fails: the label
depends on shape, which C lacks.
A strict CBM guarantees something weaker.

Its own prediction depends on the
input only through the concepts.

Whether the true label does is a
property of the chosen vocabulary.

More accurate colour and size
estimates would not help.
The fix is a richer vocabulary: add shape.
Now the two vectors differ.

Each concept value is a single
number on its way to the task head.
What exactly does that number carry?

A concept value should answer one
question: is this concept present?

Leakage is when the value
carries more than that answer,
and the task head uses the extra.
Here is a constructed example.

A plains zebra and a Grévy's
zebra both have stripes,
so both get the label stripes equals 1.

A soft predictor scores plains zebras
around 0.72, and Grévy's zebras,

with narrower and denser
stripes, around 0.96.
Both mean stripes present,

yet a threshold near 0.84
separates them almost perfectly.

The binary label alone
leaves the head at chance.

So the stripes value also
carries stripe density,
which nobody named and nobody can inspect.
That hidden part is the leakage.

Now correct a plains zebra's
stripes value to 1, its true value.

The head reads anything
above 0.84 as Grévy's zebra,

so the correct edit
gives the wrong species.

That was implicit leakage,
inside a continuous score.

Explicit leakage is a side path that
carries latent features around the concepts,

so an edit no longer controls
everything the head sees.

Ordinary variation in
confidence is not leakage.

Leakage is systematic,
and the head uses it.
Does a real trained model leak?

Take a small model trained on synthetic
shapes, which Part 11 looks at closely,

and its concept large, labelled 1
for a radius of 14 pixels or more.

Its score rises smoothly with the radius:
about 0.09 at 12 pixels, 0.25 at 13,

So it carries a graded size,
more than large or not large.

A simple linear probe recovers essentially
nothing about the shape's position or
shade from the scores.

That is how to look for leakage: probe what
the scores predict beyond their labels.
This is one small synthetic model.

Hard concepts pass only 0 or 1 to
the head, so nothing extra travels.
On our CUB run,

a linear head on hard concepts gets about
53 percent of the test photos right;
on soft scores, 69 percent.

Independent training fits the
head on true binary concepts,

so it never learns hidden
detail in the scores.

Side paths can be removed,
or reported clearly.
Above all, measure: probe the scores,

and test whether interventions
help on held-out data.

The original concept bottleneck needs a
person to label every concept on every
training image.

That is its main cost, and most
newer methods try to reduce it.

One supervised training record
looks like this: the image,

a 0 or 1 for each named
concept, and the class.

On CUB, that meant 112
concept labels per photograph.

The newer methods form a ladder
of shrinking supervision.

On the first rung, CBMs and concept
embedding models need the image,
the concept labels and the class.

Post-hoc models, label-free models, LaBo
and VLG-CBM drop the concept labels.

Classification by description
drops training altogether.

An everyday way to read the ladder
is to ask who supplies the concepts.
Think of learning to recognise animals.

On rung one, a tutor marks
every feature on every picture.

On rung two, an experienced spotter,
a pretrained model, does the looking,

and a field guide, a language model or
a list of phrases, supplies the names.

On rung three, only the
field guide is left:
a language model writes the descriptions,

and CLIP simply compares
them with each photo.

Each step up saves labelling,
and it also removes a check.

A tutor who ticks a box
has looked at the picture.

On the higher rungs, nobody checks
the concepts against the photos.

So for each variant,
watch for one question:

who checks that a named concept
is really visible in the image?

We come back to it when
we discuss grounding.

Newer variants change four things:
where the concepts come from,

how each concept is detected, how it is
represented, and what reaches the task head.

We will walk through them on one
running example: photographs of zebras,

horses and giraffes,
the classes from Part 4.
We train on 24 photos and test on 12.

For each variant, we first say in one line
what changed compared with the plain CBM.

Then we write down how the path changes:
from x, the image, to c hat, the concepts,
to y hat, the class.
First, Concept Embedding Models.

One number per concept is a narrow channel,
and when the vocabulary is incomplete,
accuracy suffers, as we saw in Part 8.
Here is the intuition.
Give each concept two prototypes,

typical points that stand for stripes
present and for stripes absent.

The probability works like a dimmer switch
that slides the concept between the two.

Both prototypes are computed
from the image itself,

so they can differ from
one photo to the next.

That lets detail beyond yes
or no travel to the head.
Now the mechanics.

An embedding is a short list of
numbers that describes something;
here each one has two numbers.

From the image, the model computes
two embeddings for every concept:

one describing it as
active, one as inactive.

It also predicts the probability,
p, that the concept is present.

Suppose that, as in Part 4, it misses
the stripes on this photo: p is only 0.1.

The concept's embedding mixes the
two: p times the active embedding,
plus one minus p times the inactive one.

With p equal to 0.1, take the first
entry: 0.1 × 0.82, plus 0.9 × 0.22,
gives 0.28.

The second entry works the same way, and
the mixed vector sits close to inactive.

The head, a linear layer as in Part 4, reads
all three concepts, six numbers in all.

The stripes vector says inactive,
so the head favours horse.

To intervene, a person
sets p, not the vector.

Setting p to 1 swaps in the active
embedding, and zebra now leads.
During training,

CEM randomly replaces some predicted
probabilities with their true values,

about one concept in four, so the head
learns to respond to corrections.

The gain is capacity: a vector can
carry detail that one number cannot.
When does that matter?
Recall Part 8.
With only colour and size as concepts,

the blue circle and the blue square
got the same concept values,
so no head could tell them apart.

With embeddings, the vector for
blue is computed from each image,

so it can differ between
the circle and the square.

Shape can then reach the head
without ever being named.

The cost is inspectability: the
coordinates of that vector have no names,

so part of what the head
uses cannot be inspected.

The detail that separated the circle from
the square is exactly the part nobody can
read.

Compared with the plain CBM,
two of the four things changed.

Each concept is now a vector
instead of one number,
and the head reads those vectors.

People still label every concept, and
a trained predictor still detects them.

In symbols, for concept j out of k: g now
outputs a probability and two embeddings,
each m numbers long.

c hat j is the mixed vector,
and f reads all of them.

Training still needs images,
concept labels and class labels.

Second, post-hoc concept
bottleneck models.

Instead of training a concept
predictor from scratch,

they reuse a pretrained
encoder that already exists,

so nobody labels concepts
on the training images.
First, the intuition.

A pretrained encoder already arranges
photos in its feature space,

and some directions in that
space follow visual properties,
such as how striped an animal is.

A concept bank gives names
to some of those directions.
A concept score then asks one question:

how far along the stripes
direction is this photo?
Now the details.

Here the frozen encoder
is CLIP's image encoder:

each photograph becomes 512
numbers, which we call e of x.
Where does a direction come from?
Yuksekgonul and colleagues use two routes.

The first is a concept activation
vector, as in TCAV in Part 1:

separate the features of images with and
without the concept by a linear boundary,
and take the direction across it.

It needs some labelled
examples for each concept,
but no labels on the training images.

The second route needs no
example images at all.

CLIP's text encoder places a phrase
in the same space as the images,
so the phrase itself gives the direction.

We take the text route, with a
concept bank of eight phrases,

from black and white
stripes to a wooden fence.
Each phrase becomes a direction, v j.

How far along a direction
does a photo lie?

Multiply the features and the direction
entry by entry, then add up the products:
this is the dot product.

With just two entries, it is
the first entry times the first,
plus the second times the second.

A concept score is this projection,
computed over all 512 entries,
once for each of the eight directions.

Both vectors have length one,
so each score is also a cosine.

The raw scores sit close together,
so each one is standardised.

Subtract its average over the 24 training
photos, then divide by its spread,
the standard deviation.
For stripes, that gives 1.41.

For this zebra photo, black and
white stripes scores highest,

1.4 standard deviations above its
average on the training photos.

A linear head is then trained with
the class labels, on 24 photos.

As in Part 4, each class score is a row
of weights times the concept scores,

plus a constant, b, and a softmax
turns the scores into shares.
The head is also sparse.

An L1 penalty adds the size
of every weight to the loss,

so weights that do not help
are pushed to exactly zero.

Of 24 possible weights, 8 concepts
times 3 classes, only 4 are non-zero:

zebra reads stripes, giraffe reads a long
neck, and horse reads a flowing mane.

For this zebra, only the stripes
weight feeds the zebra score:

the stripes score times its weight,
plus the constant, gives about 2.03.

The softmax turns the three scores
into shares, and zebra gets 0.77.

All 12 held-out photos
are classified correctly.

This is a tiny teaching
example, not a benchmark.

Lower the stripes score to its
usual value on other animals,
and zebra falls to 0.14.

The hybrid version,
PCBM-h, adds a residual:

a second linear model that reads the raw
features and recovers what the concepts
miss.

Its class scores are added to the
head's scores before the softmax.
Why does that help?

Eight phrases cannot describe
everything the encoder sees,
and the residual picks up the rest.

In the paper, PCBM-h comes close to the
original model on every dataset reported,

while the pure concept
model falls further behind.
The same side path weakens interventions.

An edit changes a concept score, but the
residual reads the raw features directly,

so it keeps its vote for zebra
whatever we write in the stripes slot.
On our photo, after the same edit,

the hybrid still gives
zebra 0.20 rather than 0.14,

because part of its evidence never
passed through a named concept.

Compared with the plain CBM,
three of the four things changed.

The concepts come from a bank
of phrases instead of people,

a frozen encoder and a projection
replace the trained predictor,

and in the hybrid a residual
also reaches the head.
Each concept is still one number.
In symbols, for concept j out of k:

g is a frozen encoder followed by a
projection onto the direction v j.

f is sparse and linear, plus
a residual, r, in the hybrid.

Only f is trained, from
images and class labels.

The third variant is the label-free
concept bottleneck model.

A supervised bottleneck needs a person
to label every concept on every photo,
112 of them for each bird in CUB.

Label-free models need
no human concept labels.
Here is the intuition.

CLIP is the teacher: it has learned
from images paired with captions,

so it can score how well any
phrase matches any image.

The student is a frozen ResNet
with one linear layer on top,

and it learns to copy
the teacher's scores.

A language model writes the exam
questions: the phrases to score.
The method has five steps.

The language model proposes phrases,
CLIP filters and scores them,

the student learns to copy the
scores, and a sparse final layer,

trained with the class labels,
turns them into a class.

Step one: ask a language model, for each
class, for its most important features,

the things commonly seen around
it, and its superclasses,
the broader groups it belongs to.

Here is the real reply for zebra
to the first question, as JSON.

Three questions for each of three
classes give 59 candidate concepts.
Step two: filter.

Phrases that contain a class name go,
such as zebras or horse-like body.

Equine goes as a near-duplicate
of equine animal.

Leather saddle and ossicones on head go
because even the photos that match them
best score low with CLIP.
34 concepts remain.

Step three: CLIP scores every image
against every remaining concept.

A higher score means the
phrase fits the image better.

These scores are the teacher's
answers: targets for the student,
not labels from a person.
Step four builds the student.

A different frozen network, here
a ResNet-50 rather than CLIP,

turns each image into 2048
features, written e of x.

A linear layer, W c, maps them
to 34 concept activations.

This layer is often called the projection,
and it is the only part that learns.

The teacher's scores and the student's
activations come on different scales,

so both are standardised: subtract
the average over the photos,

then divide by the spread,
the standard deviation.
For this zebra,

CLIP's stripes score sits 1.41
standard deviations above its average,

and the student's stripes
activation sits 1.36 above.
What does copying mean?
Take one concept, black and white stripes.
Across many images,

the student's activation should be
high where CLIP's score is high,
and low where it is low.

Only this pattern across images
matters, not the exact values.

Before the comparison, every
standardised value is cubed:
multiplied by itself three times.
Cubing stretches the extremes:

a score two standard deviations
above average becomes eight,

while half a standard deviation
shrinks to one eighth.

So the images that CLIP scores
highest count the most.

To compare two lists of numbers, we use
the cosine: multiply them entry by entry,
add up, and divide by the two lengths.

It is 1 when the lists rise and fall
together, even if one is twice the other,

near 0 when they are unrelated, and negative
when they move in opposite directions.

Now the match for concept
j, such as stripes.

Let q bar be the student's standardised
activations across the images,
and P bar for CLIP's standardised scores.

The match is the cosine
between their cubes.

W c is trained to make this
match large for every concept.

It needs no labels, so every
unlabelled photo can help.

Step five: a final layer from concepts to
classes, trained with the class labels.

An L1 penalty on the weights pushes
most of them to exactly zero,
which is what sparse means.
6 of 102 weights survive.

Zebra reads black and white stripes,
and giraffe reads extremely long neck.

Horse reads muscular equine
build and riding bridle,
and safari vehicles counts against it.
Here is one prediction.

For this zebra, the zebra score is 1.46
times the stripes activation, 1.36,

plus a little from wildebeest herds
and a small constant: 2.02 in all.
Horse gets −0.4 and giraffe about 0.
As shares, zebra gets 0.82.
Why insist on sparsity?
A dense layer would use all 102 weights,

and nobody can check 102
numbers behind every decision.
Six weights can be read in a few seconds,

and each one is a claim a
person can check, such as:
black and white stripes count for zebra.
Reading them also shows a risk.

Riding bridle, safari vehicles and
wildebeest herds describe the setting,

not the animal, so the head
uses context as evidence.

A horse photographed beside a safari
vehicle would lose evidence for horse.

Compared with the plain
concept bottleneck,

a language model names the
concepts instead of a person,

and the concept layer learns to copy CLIP
instead of learning from concept labels.

The head is still trained
with class labels.

So label-free does not mean
unsupervised: the language model,

CLIP and the class
labels all supervise it.

In symbols: g is the frozen backbone e
followed by the learned linear layer W c,

fitted to CLIP's scores
with the cosine of cubes.
f is a sparse linear layer.

The data: images and class
labels, no concept labels.

Label-free models train a
linear layer to imitate CLIP.

Fourth, LaBo, short for
Language in a Bottle,
asks a language model for concepts too,

but keeps CLIP itself as
the concept detector.
The intuition is simple.

Describe each class in a few short
sentences, let CLIP read them,

and use its similarity scores
directly as the concepts,
written as 100 times CLIP's cosine.
For our zebra photo,

the stripes sentence scores higher than
the mane sentence and the neck sentence.
The method has four steps.

A language model writes sentences, a
selection rule keeps the most useful ones,

CLIP scores each image against them,
and a linear head, started from a guess,
turns the scores into a class.

In step one, the language model writes
eight short sentences for each class,
as JSON.
Here they are for zebra.
Which sentences should we keep?

First, each one should separate
its class from the others.

Take a sentence's average CLIP
score on the zebra training photos,

and subtract its average
on the best other class.

Bold black and white stripes has
the widest margin of the eight.

Stocky horse-like body matches
another class better than zebras,
so it separates nothing.

Second, the set should not say
the same thing three times.
Once one stripes sentence is in,

a second stripes sentence
adds much less that is new.
Step two puts numbers on both ideas.

Discriminability is the
margin from two slides back,

rescaled within the class so that the best
sentence gets 1 and the worst gets 0.
Large striped ears lands at 0.66.

Coverage gain measures what a sentence
adds beyond the sentences already chosen.

A greedy rule builds the
set one sentence at a time:
each round it takes the best mix,

0.7 times discriminability plus 0.3 times
coverage gain, and keeps that choice.

In round one, bold black and white
stripes scores 0.7 × 1, plus 0.3 × 0.69,
which is 0.91, the best of the eight.

Unique facial stripe patterns comes
second, then large striped ears.
For horse, a long flowing mane leads.

For giraffe, an extremely
long vertical neck.

Step three: CLIP scores the image
against the nine chosen sentences.
Those nine numbers are the bottleneck.

Score j compares CLIP's encoding
of the image, phi of x,

with its encoding of
sentence j, psi of s j.

Step four: a linear layer from sentences
to classes, started from a language prior,
a starting guess taken from the sentences.

Each class gives one third to
each of its own three sentences,
and nothing to the others.

So each class score is the average
of its own three sentence scores.

For this zebra, zebra gets 28.1,
horse 22.9 and giraffe 23.7.

As shares, zebra gets 0.98, and 11
of the 12 test photos are right.
Why start from a prior?

A head that starts from zero must learn
from the labels which sentence belongs to

which class, and that is hard
with few labelled photos.
The prior already encodes it.

A linear probe is a linear layer on
CLIP's image features, with no concepts.

The LaBo paper reports its clearest advantage
over a linear probe with one labelled
photo per class.

After that, training with the class
labels moves the weights a little,
and then all 12 are right.

Notice the zebra sentences:
all three are about stripes.

Is CLIP detecting striped ears, or
stripes anywhere in the picture?
The scores alone cannot tell.

Compared with the plain
concept bottleneck,

a language model writes the concepts as
sentences, and CLIP scores them directly,
so nothing is trained to detect concepts.

Only the head learns, and it starts from
the language prior instead of from scratch.
In symbols: g is CLIP itself,

so c hat j is 100 times the cosine
between the image and sentence j.

f is a linear layer that starts
from the language prior.
The data: images and class labels.

Label-free models and
LaBo share a weakness:

nothing checks that a concept is
actually visible in the image.
The fix rests on a simple intuition.

Naming a concept is not
the same as pointing at it.

So ask a detector to point at
each concept in the image,
and count only the concepts it can find.
There are three ways a concept can fail.

Some are not visual,
such as a gull's call.
Some describe the setting, not the bird.

And some score highly on images
that do not contain them,

such as a black head on a
gull whose head is white.

Srivastava and colleagues point out that
a head built on a set of random concepts

can reach accuracy
comparable to these models.

So the concept scores were carrying
information that their names do not describe,
a form of the leakage we met in Part 9.

Their method, VLG-CBM,
grounds the concepts first.

It uses an open-vocabulary
object detector:

a detector that can search
for any phrase you give it,
not only a fixed list of objects.

It looks for each concept in each training
image, and draws a box where it finds it.

A concept counts as present
only where a box was found.

For our gull, the bill, head and wingtips
each get a one, and the call gets a zero.

We call this vector c det: the
concept labels from the detector.

These grounded labels
train the concept layer:

a linear layer that turns the backbone's
features into one score per concept.

The loss is a binary cross-entropy,
as in the original CBM,
but no person draws the labels.
One term, as in Part 5.

The wingtips have a box, so their label
is one; if the layer predicts 0.8,
the term is −log 0.8, about 0.22.

The call has no box, so its label is
zero; a prediction of 0.2 costs the same,
minus log of one −0.2.

They also report the number of
effective concepts, NEC for short.

Each row of the head holds one
class's weights, one per concept.

Count the non-zero weights in each
row, here three, two and four,

and average over the
classes: the NEC is three.
Why does this count matter?

A head that puts weight on every
concept can fit almost anything.
The paper proves that even a random,

untrained concept layer can approximate
any linear classifier once there are enough
concepts.

So a dense head can be accurate
and still explain nothing.

So the fair comparison gives
every model the same budget:
the same number of concepts per class.

Only then does higher accuracy say
something about the concepts themselves.

In symbols, the count for class k is
the zero norm of its row of weights:
the number of entries that are not zero.

The NEC averages that
count over the K classes.

The paper reports accuracy
with the NEC held at five.
A head like that can actually be read:

each class rests on a
handful of named concepts.

Compared with label-free
models, two things change.

The concept layer learns from the detector's
boxes instead of copying CLIP's scores,

and the head is judged at a fixed
number of concepts per class.

In symbols: g is a backbone
with a concept layer, W c,
trained on the detector labels c det.

f is sparse and linear, with the number
of effective concepts held fixed.

The data: images and class
labels, plus a detector.

The last step on the ladder
removes training altogether.

Menon and Vondrick call it
classification by description.
The intuition is a checklist.

A language model writes a short
checklist for every class.

CLIP ticks each item softly, with a
score for how well the photo matches it.
The class with the best average tick wins.

A language model writes a few
descriptors for every class:

short phrases about what
the class looks like.

For a herring gull: a white body with
black wingtips, a yellow beak and legs,
a red spot on its beak.

CLIP scores the image against each
descriptor: that score is the soft tick.

The class score is simply the
average of its descriptors' scores,
and the highest average wins.
Where does a score come from?
CLIP has two encoders.

One, phi, turns the image into
a vector; the other, psi,

turns the descriptor into
a vector in the same space.

The score is the cosine
similarity of the two:

near one when they point the same
way, smaller when they do not.

Then y hat k, the score of class k,
averages the descriptor scores over D k,
the class's list of descriptors.
Nothing is fitted to the target data.

Every prediction comes with its reasons:
the descriptor scores that were averaged.
On our gull photograph,

the five herring gull descriptors
score between 0.32 and 0.34,
and their average is about 0.33.

But the slaty-backed gull's
descriptors average slightly higher,
so it edges ahead by a tiny margin.

Our photo shows a herring gull, so
this prediction is a near miss.

On all of CUB, the descriptors help
only slightly over plain class names,

where CLIP compares the photo with
the species name alone: in our run,
53.1 percent against 52.9.
So when is this attractive?
When you have no labelled images at all.

And a new class needs only a new
description: write its checklist,

and it can be scored at
once, with no retraining.

But the descriptors
themselves can be wrong:

the language model says a California gull
has a black head, which it does not.
That is one of several risks.

A descriptor can also be non-visual: no
single photo shows a bird's wingspan.

It can describe the setting
rather than the bird.

And nobody checks the ticks: CLIP gives
every item some score, true or not.

Compared with LaBo, the
head is no longer learned.

LaBo trained a linear layer
on CLIP's sentence scores;
here the class score is a fixed average,

so nothing is trained and no
labelled image is needed.

In symbols: g is CLIP, c hat d is
the similarity to descriptor d,

and f is a fixed average over
each class's descriptors.
The data: none.

The cost: nothing guarantees that the
descriptors are correct, or grounded.

Six variants are a lot
to hold in mind at once.

This table puts them beside the
original CBM, one row per method,
and we fill it one column at a time.

The first column is the
data needed for training.

Here x is an image, c its concept
labels, and y its class label.

Supervised CBMs and concept
embedding models need all three.

Post-hoc models, label-free models, LaBo
and VLG-CBM drop the concept labels.

Classification by description, CBD in
the table, needs no training data at all.

The second column says
who supplies the concepts.

For CBMs and concept embedding models,
people do, through their labels.

The others take them from a concept bank,
a language model, CLIP, or a detector.

The third column is what the
task head actually reads.

A CBM passes one number per concept, a
concept embedding model a vector per concept,

and a post-hoc model its
projection scores plus a residual.

Label-free models and VLG-CBM pass the
outputs of a learned concept layer,

and LaBo and classification by
description pass raw CLIP scores.
The last column is what gets trained.

CBMs and concept embedding models train
the concept predictor and the head.

Post-hoc models and LaBo
train only the head.

Label-free models and VLG-CBM
train a concept layer and the head.

Classification by description
trains nothing at all.

Each change makes concepts cheaper
or predictions more accurate.
None makes grounding automatic.

A phrase from a language
model, or a CLIP similarity,

does not show that the model
sees that property in the image.
That has to be checked.

One question sums up the table: who
supplies the concepts, and who checks them?

In CBMs and concept embedding
models, people label the concepts,
so people check them.

In post-hoc models, a concept bank supplies
them, checked only by whoever built it.

Label-free models and LaBo take
them from a language model,
and only a CLIP similarity checks them.

VLG-CBM keeps the language model,
and adds a detector as the check.

In classification by
description, nobody checks.
This is the general trade-off.

Each rung up the ladder removes a human
labour cost, and with it a human check.

The labour saved on labelling
has to be spent later,

on checking that the concepts
are really in the image.
How should we judge such a model?

Accuracy alone hides most of what matters,
so we ask four separate questions,
each about a different part of the model.

First, task accuracy: are
the predictions correct?

In everyday terms, is
the final answer right?

Measure it on held-out test images, images
the model never saw during training.
The formula only counts.

The bracket is 1 when the prediction matches
the true label, and 0 when it does not.

Add up the ones and divide
by the number of images.

Three predictions with two right
give an accuracy of two thirds.

Second, concept accuracy: are
the concept estimates correct?

In everyday terms, did the model
read the evidence correctly?
Take one test image, a small red square.

Round each concept score to 0 or
1, and compare it with the label.

Large scores 0.78, which rounds to 1, but
the square is small, so its label is 0.
Four of the five match.

Concept accuracy averages these matches
over all images and all concepts.

The second question has
a second half, grounding:

does each estimate rest
on the intended evidence?

A score for wingtip black should come
from the wingtip, not from the water.
So we also check where the detector looks.

Third, faithfulness: does the output
actually depend on the concepts,
in the way the model claims?

An explanation is faithful when it tells
the truth about how the answer was made.

To test it, change a concept and check
that the output moves as the head says.
In the gull head from Part 2,

setting wingtip black to 1 lifts
herring gull from 0.29 to 0.91.

Fourth, intervention utility:
when a person corrects a concept,

do decisions improve,
and at what human cost?

Correct concepts one at a time, and plot
accuracy against the number of corrections.

Each correction costs a person's time,
so a curve that rises early is better.

Here is a real experiment where
we know every true concept.

The images are synthetic, 64 × 64
pixels: each shape is red or blue,
a circle or a square, small or large.

Two colours, two shapes and
two sizes give eight classes.

Five yes-or-no concepts describe each
image: red, blue, circle, square and large.
Together they fully determine the class.

Three models share the same
small CNN, the same data,

and the same training budget
of 60 epochs, that is,
60 passes through the 768 training images.
The black box predicts the class directly.

The multi-task model also
predicts the concepts,
with a concept head beside its class head.

The strict CBM predicts
the concepts first,
and its head reads only those five values.

Each bar is the share of the 512
test images classified correctly:

78.7 percent for the black box, 82.0 for
multi-task, and 81.6 for the strict CBM.

On this question alone, the
three look about the same.
Over all images and all five concepts,

the strict CBM gets 92.4 percent
of its concept values right.

The bars on the left
split this by concept.

Colour is always right,
and shape is hardest,

at about 84 percent for
circle and 83 for square.

Back to our test image,
the small red square.

Its concept large reads 0.78, so the

A person sets large to 0, and the same

Now do this for every test image.

The true labels play a perfect

It fixes the concept with

For our square, that is large, which

On this chart, the horizontal axis counts

With all five corrected, it reaches 100.

Now pick the concept to

The shaded band spans the lowest

Now the multi-task model.

Edit its concept head, and its
class scores stay exactly the same,

because its class head
never reads the concepts.

Read these numbers with care: one training
seed, meaning a single training run,

512 synthetic test images, and
corrections taken from the true labels,

standing in for a perfect,
effortless expert.

Real experts make mistakes,
and their time is costly.
The three models have similar accuracy,

yet they differ completely
in intervention utility.
Each metric measures a different property.

Why can similar accuracy hide
such different behaviour?

Accuracy marks only the final
answer, not the route to it.

The multi-task model's class head
never reads its concept estimates,

so fixing one is like correcting
a note that nobody reads.

In the strict CBM, the concepts
are the only road to the answer,
so a fix reaches the prediction.

So far our inputs were
photographs of birds.

Concept bottlenecks fit wherever experts
already reason with named findings,

the things they check
and write down by name.
In medicine,

Koh and colleagues also trained a CBM
on knee X-rays from the Osteoarthritis
Initiative.

The model first scores
ten clinical findings,

such as joint space narrowing and bone
spurs, each on a small scale of its own.

From those, the head predicts
how severe the osteoarthritis is,
on four levels from 0 to 3.

A radiologist can correct a finding,
and the grade is recomputed.

Here, joint space narrowing goes from
1 to 2, and the grade goes from 2 to 3.

Radiologists already write
their reports in these terms.

In language, the CEBaB benchmark annotates
restaurant reviews with four concepts:
food, service, ambiance and noise.

In this review the food is praised
and the service is criticised,

while ambiance and
noise are not mentioned.

Text bottleneck models predict the
star rating from those concept values,
so you can see which aspect drove it.
Reviewers already write this way.
In intensive care,

Wu and colleagues built concept
bottlenecks on patients' time series,
measurements recorded over time.

The task is vasopressor onset: when
a patient will need vasopressors,
drugs that support blood pressure.

The concepts are summaries
learned without concept labels,

close to how doctors
already sum up a patient,

in terms like illness
severity and kidney function.
In wearable sensing,

X-CHAR explains a complex activity through
the simpler activities it is made of,

which a person can recognise
in the sensor signal.

In its nurse data, the simple
activities include check vitals,
collect blood and oral care.

People already describe a complex activity
as the simple steps it is made of.

And in sleep staging, the concepts are
the patterns that scorers already use,

as in Part 6: spindles,
K-complexes and slow waves.

The head turns them into a
sleep stage, such as stage two.

Scorers already mark
these patterns by hand,

so each concept matches
a mark they would make.
The recipe is the same each time.

Name the findings an expert checks,
predict them from the raw signal,
and let the decision depend on them alone.

Readable concepts in the middle
do not guarantee a good model.

Let us follow the path from the photo
x, through the concept scores c hat,

to the answer y hat, and ask what
can fail at each of five points.

First, distribution shift: the encoder
meets data unlike its training data.

In symbols, new inputs come from a different
distribution than the training inputs.
Recall the chest X-ray model from Part 1.

Its AUC, a score where 1 means perfect
ranking and 0.5 means guessing,

was about 0.93 on X-rays from
the hospitals it learned from,
and about 0.82 at a new hospital.

In practice, the model looks fine where it
was built and does worse at the new site.

Second, wrong grounding: the concept
detector responds to the wrong evidence,

such as the water behind a
gull instead of its wingtip.

In practice, the score looks
right for the wrong reason,
until a gull turns up away from water.

Third, missing information: the vocabulary
leaves out what the task needs.

In Part 8, a blue circle and a blue
square shared one concept vector,

so the best any head could do
was guess, right half the time.

In practice, two cases an expert would
tell apart look identical to the head.

Fourth, the task head can
learn the wrong relationship.
Recall the billing head from Part 7:

it takes away 2 for each unit of
duplicate charge, the wrong sign.

A correct edit sets duplicate charge to
1, and billing falls from 0.80 to 0.45.

In practice, the expert's fix is right,
yet the decision moves the wrong way.

Fifth, the intervention can
be wrong, or too costly.

On this chart from Part 11, each step to
the right is one more correction per image,

and each correction
takes an expert's time.

Ours came from true labels,
an expert who never errs.

In practice, a busy expert
can misjudge a concept too,

and every check uses time
they could spend elsewhere.

So ask five questions of
any concept bottleneck.
Are the concepts meaningful?
Are they grounded correctly?
Are they sufficient for the task?
Does the model actually use them?
And do corrections improve decisions?

Knab and colleagues' 2026 survey
organises the field around the same parts:

the input, the concepts,
the output and the training.

It lists these issues
among its open challenges.
One last time, the gull.

A black box maps the photograph
straight to a species.
Open it up.
Input.
Encoder.
Concept predictor.
Named concepts.
Task head.
Prediction.

A person sees that the wingtips are
black and corrects that concept.

The head now says American
herring gull, at 0.91.

But the interface is only as good as
its parts: the concepts it names,

where they look, and the
head that reads them.

A concept may be missing, a
detector may look at the water,
and a head may hold a wrong rule.
In short,

concept bottleneck models put named values
that people can read in the middle of a
prediction.

Those values can be inspected,
evaluated, and sometimes corrected.

The challenge is to make sure the interface
faithfully represents the information
on which the prediction depends.

Put simply, whatever the answer uses
should be visible in the concepts.
Four things to remember.

Post-hoc methods explain
a model after the fact,
